Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I am glad you made that clarification because I had a different interpretation of your remarks. I appreciate your second statement because it does, for me, qualify the interpretation I originally had of your first submission. So I thank you very much for rising in your place and explaining that very important point to me.
Of those paying their own drug costs, 29 per cent paid between $50 and $100 a month, and 18 per cent paid over $100. On an annual basis this represents a direct cost of between $600 and several thousand dollars to each of these people. That is a phenomenal amount of money for those people to have to pay.
Of the 16 most commonly used drugs by respondents, eight had generic or other competition. Savings achieved by the use of cheaper equivalents ranged from 21 per cent to 89 per cent. The proportion of drugs with competition in any future list will decrease if amendments to the Patent Act are passed.
This presentation, which is neither against nor for the legislation, assesses very reasonably the shortcomings in Bill C-22. It should be read in its entirety by all Hon. Members in order that they will have a better and fuller appreciation of what is taking place.
The Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops also wrote to the Minister. I believe it was the Bishop of Calgary, Paul J. O'Byrne, who wrote to the Minister expressing his concerns about Bill C-22. I should like to read part of his submission to destroy the very weak argument and comment of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) that the opposition to the Bill is in the imagination of opposition Members of Parliament. He wrote the following:

May 5, 1987
Patent Act
We have followed the debate on this legislation and have noted that the pressure to change Canada's generic drug laws has not come from the people of this country. Indeed, national organizations representing thousands of Canadians from virtually all sectors of society have been unanimous in calling upon your Government not to proceed with the proposed legislation.
We add our voice to that call because we believe that this legislation, if enacted, would have detrimental effects on average Canadians, especially on the elderly and the poor. Thanks in large part to existing drug patent legislation, Canadians enjoy low prescription drug prices and high standards of health care.
The proposed amendments will cost Canadians hundreds of millions of dollars annually in drug price increases. The changes will also have serious implications for health care costs and for the future of medicare in this country.
The letter goes on, but basically it asks the Government to withdraw the Bill for many of the reasons which Members of Parliament, ordinary citizens, and other Canadians have expressed about the effects of Bill C-22.
We on the committee were not only limited to receiving briefs and presentations from individuals who appeared before us. We also received numerous presentations from individuals who could not attend. One such group was from the Province of Quebec, the ACEF-Centre, Association Cooperative D'Economie Familiale du Centre de Montreal. It indicated the following opinion:
-Bill C-22, an Act to amend the Patent Act, should be withdrawn.
By making it impossible for pharmaceutical companies to copy drug products quickly, the bill would result in the medium term in the consumer having to pay more for prescription drugs. Indeed, the consumer would end up paying more, either directly at the pharmacy or in taxes or medical insurance premiums.
Furthermore, the ACEF-Centre believes that this bill does not deal directly with the real problems affecting the pharmaceutical industry, namely the overabundance of similar, useless and even harmful drugs on the market, the lack of research to develop drugs that are truly effective in treating illnesses which are now incurable, the excessively high percentage of funds allocated for advertising purposes, etc.
Another distinguished Canadian organization of professional people opposes the thrust of Bill C-22.
On several occasions the Minister said to the House that he had two resolutions from the Province of Quebec supporting the thrust of Bill C-22. 1 do not doubt it. However, it is interesting to note that other legislatures or assemblies in different provinces have also had the subject matter of Bill C-22 before them.
I do not wish to downplay the significance and importance of the resolution from the National Assembly of the Province of Quebec, because it is an important one, but equally so I would have thought that a Minister of the Crown would have availed himself of the opportunity to express very clearly what other legislatures have done.
The Minister of Health and Social Services in Prince Edward Island and the Minister of Justice and Attorney General wrote a letter to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) in November, 1986, in which they said:
This Government is strongly opposed to any amendments which will result in an increase in the cost of prescription drugs. While this position was conveyed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs at the Minister's Conference in Thunder Bay, we feel it is necessary to reiterate it in writing.
To date, we have no guarantee that the proposed amendments will result in any economic benefit to the Province of Prince Edward Island or that the provincial drug bill will not increase because of these amendments.
One of the persons who sent that letter was the Liberal Minister of Health of the Province of Prince Edward Island. As well, the Legislature of Prince Edward Island convened a session and, by unanimous consent, passed a resolution in opposition to Bill C-22, which I should like to read into the record. For whatever reasons, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs failed to make mention of the matter in his deliberations. I am not suggesting that he did not want to give balance to his argument. He just wanted us to hear only one side! I hope to give balance to the argument and to put both sides of it before the House. The resolution reads:
WHEREAS the Government of Canada has introduced amendments to the Patent Act which will inexorably over time result in an increase in the price of prescription drugs;
AND WHEREAS the Province of Prince Edward Island has recently introduced a Drug Cost Assistance Plan which strives to reduce the cost-burden of drugs for senior citizens;
AND WHEREAS increased prescription costs will adversely affect this Plan and indeed all other citizens of our Province who require drugs from time to time;
AND WHEREAS there is no more than a token, non-statutory requirement in the proposed federal scheme for pharmaceutical manufacturers to meet any research and development expenditure commitments;
AND WHEREAS there is no direct economic benefit which will accrue to Prince Edward Island as a result of the proposed amendments;
AND WHEREAS this Government is committed to obtaining prescription drugs at the lowest possible cost to the citizens of Prince Edward Island;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that this Assembly urge the Prime Minister in the strongest possible terms not to proceed with this Bill.
That was Resolution No. 6 regarding the Patent Act dated March 10, 1987, passed by the Legislature of Prince Edward Island. However, the Minister rose and spoke as if they did not even exist, as if the senior citizens, the elderly, and the other people of that province did not count for anything.
I think it is a very important document, just as important as the one from the National Assembly of the Province of Quebec. I hope Hon. Members give due consideration to what the people of both those provinces are saying through their elected representatives.
I have another resolution opposing Bill C-22 which was passed by another legislature. It is of great importance. Again, because of the Minister's refusal to look at both sides of the issue, he did not draw attention to it in his deliberations. I am not suggesting that he did it intentionally, because that would be unparliamentary. However, I have a telex from the Clerk of the Manitoba Legislative Assembly which was addressed to the Hon. Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and to all Members of the House of Commons which reads:
May 5, 1987

The Manitoba Legislative Assembly has directed me to send you the following resolution which it adopted on Wednesday, April 29, 1987.
The resolution reads:
Whereas the availability of safe pharmaceuticals at reasonable cost is fundamental to the health and well-being of Canadians, and
Whereas Section 41(4) of the Patent Act as amended in 1969 has provided the vehicle whereby Canadian licencees can produce low-priced generic substitutions of brand-name pharmaceuticals to be marketed in Canada, and
Whereas according to the Eastman Commission, these generic substitutions saved Canadians well over $200 million in 1983, and
Whereas these generic substitutions resulted in a saving in hospital, pharmacare and prescription costs for Manitobans amounting to over $14 million in 1986, and
Whereas the drug reimbursement paid out by the provincial Government through its universal pharmacare program has risen from $4.3 million in 1975 to $28 million in 1986, and
Whereas the proposed changes to the Patent Act which delay the introduction of new generic substitutions will result in even higher hospital, pharmacare and prescription costs, while providing few alternative benefits to Canadians, and
Whereas the cost to Manitobans of the delayed entry of new generic substitutions will be over $2 million in the first year after the changes, and could total $44 million by 1995, and
Whereas the increased costs will be borne directly by consumers both at the counter and through increased costs to our pharmacare program and will especially affect the elderly and those who require continuous medication, and
Whereas the federal Government, in spite of strong representation by the public opposing the amendments, and in the face of constant pressure from the multinational drug companies, continues to insist on amending the Patent Act.
Therefore be it resolved that the Legislative Assembly of Manitoba urge the Government of Canada to withdraw the Bill outlining amendments to the Patent Act which would result in higher cost drugs for all Canadians, and
Be it further resolved that the Clerk of the Legislative Assembly be instructed to send copies of the resolution to the Federal Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and all other Members of Parliament.
This is signed by Mr. W.H. Remnant, Clerk of the Legislative Assembly of Manitoba. The telex number is available if it is to be tabled.
There we have another legislature in this country speaking out against the harmful effects that Bill C-22 will have upon the citizens of that particular province, namely Manitoba.
We hear this cry from other provinces. Ontario sent a letter to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs opposing the proposals of Bill C-22. He offered some possible constructive changes to the Bill, and of course the Minister dismissed them. The additional costs in Ontario will be about $35 million. The Government of Saskatchewan is opposed to Bill C-22. There was a provincial election and money for the farmers. Then Saskatchewan changed its mind. Representatives came to committee and made a presentation. I have to be fair, it was not the Minister responsible in the Province of Saskatchewan, it was the Deputy Minister of Health, I believe. He was the one who, under cross-examination by Members of Parliament, in reading through his brief had about 9 to 11 preconditions and if they were to be met, Saskatchewan would support the Bill. Fortunately, or unfortunately, when I
Patent Act
questioned him, he would not, and perhaps in all fairness, could not say that he supported or did not support the Bill as it now stood because he was representing his Minister and was not in a position to exercise that sort of ministerial discretion which we know can only be given to a Minister and not his deputy.
We have seen government representatives, organization representatives, representatives of national organizations, representatives of non-profit corporations and representatives of Canadian corporations. We have had citizens groups, the Legion and people from the Church of Canada. Numerous Canadians from all walks of life, unions and what have you, all rose in opposition to Bill C-22. Some Members may say this is sickening. I do not think the stand, the suggestions, the queries and the concerns of the United Church of Canada are sickening. I do not think that the views of the Royal Canadian Legion of Canada, of their veterans, their associated members and all other members approximating 590,000, on the subject are sickening. I think they are relevant and germane to our deliberations as we proceed with the debate on Bill C-22 and the effects the Bill will have on Canadians from coast to coast.
The Canadian Drug Manufacturers Association, which I must admit is one of the lead organizations, is opposed to Bill C-22. It has a vested interest in being opposed and we should understand that off the bat. If one looks at the Canadian pharmaceutical industry, we want to see multinational corporations in operation as well as our own Canadian generic firms. That is what we want to see, Mr. Speaker.
I have listened attentively and patiently to many claims in committee. I wish to quote briefly what a number of organizations have said on this Bill. First, the Canadian Drug Manufacturers Association said this:
-we do not think there is any real social or economic reason to change the current system of compulsory licensing. It has brought only good to Canada ... world-class industry must have six separate sectors: pure research, applied research, fine chemicals, brand name manufacturers, generic manufacturers and the new biotechnological companies.. . Bill C-22 will reduce Canada's industry to only two components and will result in whopping big reliance on foreign firms for our drugs.
That is found at pages 3:7 and 3:8 of the brief, if Members find it important enough and wish to check on it.
What does the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada say? It says:
These companies (the multinationals) have indeed made their announcements (of investments). 1 think they have also said very clearly that if the Bill is not passed, not all of this investment will go ahead, and I expect you will see evidence.
I am not saying that this is blackmail, but it is pretty close to it. It is either "you pass this legislation or we will not proceed with our investment intentions". As a Canadian parliamentarian and one interested in public policy, I find that to be a very unfortunate statement made by the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association.

May 5, 1987
Patent Act
Let me quote the Canadian Labour Congress. It says:
It is the position of the Congress that the Bill presently being debated is one that is based on political considerations and not on economic ones-
The last thing in the world the ethical manufacturers in this country want is competition.
Let me come now to the Canadian Health Coalition, another reputable national organization which has professionals in its midst and has worked with this subject matter for quite some time. The coalition said:
Our conclusion is that the only ones to benefit from Bill C-22 will be the multinational pharmaceutical companies, while the cost to Canadians, both economically and in terms of their health, will be substantial.
Next is the National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation, which said:
-we are of the opinion that Bill C-22 and the policies related to it are seriously flawed. We therefore urge the Government to withdraw this legislation.
Now I come to the National Federation of Nurses Union, which said:
Unionized Canadian nurses, as taxpayers, health care consumers, and providers, urge you to withdraw the proposed amendments. The legislation is not the right combination.
Canadian nurses are opposed to Bill C-22. As you know, Mr. Speaker, many of these nurses are the ones who have to give medication which is prescribed, if you will, by physicians in Canada.
Let me read what the Public Service Alliance of Canada had to say:
We reject the premise that Canada will be denied access to needed medication unless Bill C-22 legislates a monopoly for drug manufacturers. We also reject the argument that Canada's drug patent system is unfair to the so-called innovative companies.
Of course, the Minister would lead us to believe that anyone opposed to Bill C-22 is out to lunch. That is not fair. He did not say that, he said that those who are opposed to Bill C-22 are opposition Members of Parliament. I think 1 have provided in spades today examples of Canadians' and Canadian organizations' opposition to Bill C-22. It is not merely opposition Party Members who are opposed to Bill C-22.
Professor Kell Antoft who came before the committee said the following:
-our experience has shown the branch plant operations are not concerned with basic manufacturing primarily but with repackaging-
We need to reinforce basic research in our universities ... I do not think this will be done by increasing the profit margins of the drug industry.
-but one can speculate about the plea that they (the multinationals) are unable to support research when the parent company is obviously directing research into what they can do with their excess cash.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, numerous organizations have come forward to express their reservations about Bill C-22.
Before my colleague from the New Democratic Party joins in this debate momentarily, I will conclude by saying that it has been our contention for quite some time that the Liberal Party is very much opposed to Bill C-22. We have adopted and promote the recommendations contained in the Eastman report which provide for a period of exclusivity of four years
provided certain moneys are paid into what is known as a pharmaceutical research fund. The Eastman report has been our Party's position from day one, and I want to reiterate that that is our position. We follow the recommendations of the Eastman report very clearly.
I think there is irrefutable evidence that drug prices will rise and will rise dramatically over the next number of years. Senior citizens, the poor and the less fortunate will have to pay the price of the Government's actions. There is very little support in Canada for changing the legislation in the way the Government proposes to change it. We have heard from legislative assemblies in Prince Edward Island, Manitoba and, yes, the Province of Quebec and from numerous organizations opposed to Bill C-22. We have questioned the constitutionality of this Bill and Ministers have responded by saying that there is nothing wrong with it. I suggest that there is.
Industrial benefits will not be equally distributed. There are no guarantees that it will enforce research and development commitments. There are no enforceable guarantees of job creation. I say sincerely that the process has been wrong and has been undermined by government Members of Parliament. The substance of the Bill will have a negative effect on all Canadians and particularly the elderly, the poor and those on fixed incomes. Canadians do not support the thrust of Bill C-22. For those reasons, I am opposed to Bill C-22, and I am certain that after reflection, you too will be opposed to it, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are debating a Bill brought forward by the Conservative Government. I will not describe it as a Progressive Conservative Government because there is nothing progressive about it.
We are at third reading stage of a Bill which will wipe out the legislation enacted in 1969, legislation which amended the Patent Act as it affected the manufacture and sale of prescription drugs. Prior to 1969 when multinational drug companies controlled the entire prescription drug market, there was virtually no research done and Canadians paid the second highest prices in the world for prescription drugs, drugs which are so important to many people and particularly to the young and seniors.
A whole series of studies were done in 1967 and 1968 which proved the fact that Canadians were paying the second highest prices in the world for drugs. The legislation we enacted in 1969 permitted companies, which came to be described as generic drug companies, to receive licences from companies which had researched and developed prescription drugs after a certain period of time during which the brand name drug companies could get back the investment they made in researching, developing and producing drugs. Generic companies were permitted to produce drugs on payment of royalties to the companies which had originally developed the drugs.
May 5, 1987

The legislation that was passed in 1969 had a tremendously important effect on Canadians. The drugs produced by generic companies were sold to consumers at the retail level at prices that were usually half or less the prices paid for brand name drugs.
A few years ago when the former Liberal Government was in power, the multinational drug companies, which had always opposed the legislation because they felt it interfered with their very substantial profits, put pressure on the then Government and persuaded the then Minister, the Elon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), to appoint Professor Eastman, a professor from the University of Toronto, to study the organization of the industry and its profits and to make recommendations. Those recommendations were not tabled in the House until after the Liberal Government was defeated and the present Conservative Government was in power.
The legislation that is before us bears little resemblance to the recommendations made by Professor Eastman. Professor Eastman found that the companies were making very substantial profits, among the highest profits made by any industry in Canada. Professor Eastman told us that in 1983, the last year for which he had figures, Canadians saved $211 million as a result of the competition to multinational drug companies provided by generic companies. The professor suggested ways in which he felt the law, which had been enacted in 1969, could be amended so that multinational companies would have a little more protection but the consumers would not have to pay exorbitant prices. Those recommendations of Professor Eastman have all been virtually ignored by the Government as demonstrated in this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, the proposal of the Government as contained in this Bill was greeted with almost unanimous opposition by a host of groups from across the country which wrote to, telephoned, and visited Members of Parliament. Those positions were rejected by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) who, in innumerable speeches, claimed that there was little opposition to this Bill and that the people who opposed it did not know what they were talking about and had not looked at the facts.
In debate on this Bill at second reading stage the Minister, who believed that members of the Opposition were holding the Bill up unnecessarily, argued that the Bill should be allowed to go to committee where all the witnesses would be heard and all the evidence would be seen. At almost the first meeting of the committee a government Member moved time allocation.
The result was that only a small fraction of the groups which wanted to testify and register their opinions on the Bill were allowed to do so. The time allocated to each group was limited to 45 minutes. The committee met five times a week and heard three delegations at each meeting. In the nearly 25 years that I have been in this House I have never seen a committee restrict discussion in the way in which this committee did.
When the Bill returned to the House at report stage, a motion was moved that debate at report stage be limited to one day and at third reading stage to two days. This motion, of course, passed as a result of the Government's large majority.

May 5, 1987
The Senate
Let us clearly understand the real views of the Government of Canada. 1 find it very strange, to put it mildly, that the Minister would continue to insist that there is very little opposition to the Bill given the large number of groups from almost every segment of our society which have opposed this Bill and continue to oppose it today.
On April 22 the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops wrote to the Minister. I cannot believe that the Minister believes that this is not a responsible organization. They said in part:
We have followed the debate on this legislation and have noted that the pressure to change Canada's generic drug laws has not come from the people of this country. Indeed, national organizations representing thousands of Canadians from virtually all sectors of society have been unanimous in calling upon your government not to proceed with the proposed legislation.
We add our voice to that call because we believe that this legislation, if enacted, would have detrimental effects on average Canadians, especially on the elderly and the poor.
We heard from the Canadian Legion and the United Church. I will quote again, as 1 have done on other occasions, from a letter from Mr. Jack Penner, the President of Keystone Agricultural Producers, who wrote on behalf of that organization to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs on November 25, 1986. He said in part as follows:
-KAP members share the concerns of those who believe that extended patent protections will, by limiting the ability of drug manufacturing companies to produce generic copies by means of royalty payments, raise the prices charged to consumers for pharmaceutical drugs to unwarranted levels. Farmers and their families are, of course, part of the general consuming public, and stand to be seriously affected in any such situation.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), which seeks to abolish the Senate and create a new Senate composed of Senators elected by the people on the basis of equal representation for each province and territory.
The motion also urges the Government to initiate intergovernmental discussions to that end at the earliest opportunity.
Mr. Speaker, as Hon. Members will know, Senate reform is getting a great deal of attention these days. The subject was broached last Thursday at the First Ministers meeting at Meech Lake, as part of the discussions on the Quebec constitutional question.
The First Ministers agreed to a second round of constitutional discussions where Senate reform will be analysed in depth. The provisions of the Meech Lake Accord with respect to this second round are as follows: The accord requires that a First Ministers' Conference on the Constitution be held not less than once a year and that the first be held within 12 months of proclamation of the present amendment but not later than the end of 1988; and it provides for entrenchment in the Constitution of the following items on the agenda: Senate reform, including the functions and role of the Senate, the powers of the Senate, the method of selection of Senators, and the distribution of Senate seats. It will also include the roles and responsibilities of fisheries and other agreed upon matters.
Mr. Speaker, it also provides for entrenching in the Constitution the annual First Ministers' Conference on the Economy now held under the terms of the February 1985 Memorandum of Agreement, and finally, the Accord stipulates that until constitutional amendments regarding the Senate are accomplished, the federal Government shall appoint persons from lists of candidates provided by provinces where vacancies occur and who are acceptable to the federal Government. Once these measures have been ratified, this fact should encourage the federal and provincial governments to reach agreement on the future of the Senate. Furthermore, as a token of its good faith, the federal government has promised to allow provincial governments to participate in the selection of Senators until a reform is implemented. This provision reflects the Government's desire to ensure that the provinces will be able to participate fully in our national political life.
1 also support the decision to entrench in the Constitution the annual First Ministers Conference on the economy. As Hon. Members know, the process for holding this annual conference was set in motion in February 1985 at the Regina First Ministers' Conference.
This constitutional commitment should promote two major objectives of this Government: The pursuit of national reconciliation, and the harmonization of federal and provincial policies with due respect for provincial jurisdictions.
May 5, 1987

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to comment briefly on the other principles underlying the Meech Lake Accord.
First, the Accord acknowledges the distinctive character of Quebec within Canada, whose two major linguistic communities, one centred in but not limited to Quebec, and the other concentrated in the rest of the country but also present in Quebec, together constitute a fundamental characteristic of the Canadian federation.
The Accord also aims at providing constitutional protection for a broader version of an immigration agreement concluded with Quebec. Over the years the Government and seven provinces have concluded administrative immigration agreements taking into account their particular concerns.
The most comprehensive such agreement is the Cullen-Couture agreement made with Quebec in 1978. Under this agreement Quebec has extensive powers, based on its own selection criteria, in the choice of foreign immigrants. This agreement has proved to be quite constructive since it was first implemented, and its principles have been found satisfactory.
Pursuant to the Meech Lake Accord, Ottawa will also be able to make similar agreements with the other provinces, based on their own requirements.
In view of its distinct identity, Quebec has a vested interest in the membership of the Supreme Court. Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, that Quebec is the only province whose legal system is governed by the civil code instead of by common law, the system in effect in all other provinces and territories.
Quebec's civil code is entrenched in the Constitution and recognized by the Supreme Court Act, a federal Act that specifies that at least three of the nine justices of the Court shall be appointed from the civil bar. To be on the safe side, Quebec wants to have this safeguard entrenched in the Constitution.
The Accord provides for entrenching the Supreme Court, and the requirement that at least three of the nine justices come from Quebec, in the Constitution. Furthermore, the Accord will allow for provincial input regarding appointments to the Supreme Court. Quebec and the other provinces will thus have an important role to play in the appointment of justices selected from the members of their respective bars.
The courts have maintained for a long time that under the Constitution, Parliament can raise taxes in any manner or under any tax system it sees fit but it can also appropriate funds for any purpose whatsoever. In addition to funding the programs and activities that come under its jurisdiction, Parliament may therefore incur certain expenditures for purposes that go beyond its jurisdiction.
I am satisfied that the constitutional amendments arising from this Accord will have the effect of enhancing the legitimacy of our national institutions, with the assurance that any changes in those institutions can be made only with the consent of the majority.
The Senate

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion which stands in the name of the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) with respect to the Senate of Canada is one which has considerable appeal for me. I take the position now, as I have for a very long period of time, that in a democratic system there really ought not to be any place for an appointed body which makes the claim that it represents either individual citizens, groups of Canadians, sectors of our society or regions of the country.
It is quite true that in a democratic society there are many appointed persons, for example, judges, public servants, presidents of universities and so on. However, in no case of which 1 am aware is an appointment made in total and complete absence of any system of accountability. It is also true that having a Senate of Canada lacking the obligations of precise and structured means of accountability does not mean that we do not have many hard-working and distinguished Senators. They may impose upon themselves very rigid and demanding sets of standards. We all know that an individual who is his own boss can be the hardest taskmaster possible. In the so-called other place down the hall there are undoubtedly such individuals. On the other hand, it is equally possible that the reverse may be true. However, it is not for me or for any Hon. Member to make these kinds of judgments.
From a report prepared by the Senators themselves, it is clear they are convinced that their role, their work, their importance and their functions can only be legitimized by way of election, be it by direct election or, in my view, a less desirable method of proportional representation where the successful candidates would be drawn from Party lists.
I note that the motion calls for abolition as a prerequisite to the creation of a new Senate composed of Senators elected by the people of Canada. It would seem to me that immediate abolition would signal the Government's seriousness about Senate reform. Before a new structure can be erected, it is of course necessary to clear the site. The old order changes, making way for the new.
For a long while I was one of those who believed that abolition in and by itself would be sufficient. Today, however, I am better able to see the value of a bicameral Parliament in a federal state such as ours. A second elected Chamber can be, or could be an effective protector of regional interests. A second elected Chamber could act as a check upon the very extensive executive powers which exist in a parliamentary system such as ours.
The Hon. Member for Bow River calls for equal representation from each of the provinces and the Territories. I want to commend him most heartily for having included the Territories. So often the two great Territories of this country are neglected, forgotten and left out. For example, they were absent at the recent Meech Lake meetings at which a very significant accord was arrived at for the future of this country.

May 5, 1987
The Senate
At one point the idea of equal representation from each province and territory gave me some difficulty. I contrasted a small province and a very large province in terms of population and it gave me some difficulties. However, having been an active observer at the First Ministers' Conference on aboriginal rights, I saw the important role played by the territorial Governments there, and I saw the important role played by some of the smaller provinces, for example, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Manitoba. I also saw that where convincing and effective leadership was expected from the larger provinces they were often found to be wanting.
Professor Geraets of the University of Ottawa envisages in an article he recently wrote, which was published in The Globe and Mail, an enlarged elected Senate with the regions of the country having approximately equal representation. This is a slightly different approach from that advanced by the Hon. Member for Bow River. Professor Geraets sees the regions as being first, Atlantic Canada, second, Quebec, and third, the west. Of interest to me, leaving that aside, is Professor Geraets' suggestion that 10 additional seats ought to be established for the aboriginal people of Canada. That has a considerable amount of appeal for me.
In conclusion, I would like to raise a few questions to which I hope other speakers in this debate will provide the answers. If the Meech Lake Constitutional Accord is ratified, then provincial powers in this country are going to be greatly enhanced and the federal Government will correspondingly be enfeebled. I would like to know if an elected Senate would strengthen further the voice of the regions and the provinces at the centre, or would it find itself in competition with provincial Governments for allegiance and decision-making on matters which are vital to a particular region or province? I note, for example, that in the United States of America, a very powerful Senate has caused-not in all cases but in many-state Governments to be diminished in both their authority and influence.
1 ask also what the effects of a powerful elected Senate would be on the authority and functions of this House? It would undoubtedly change us in many ways. However, I still say that if ever an institution stood in need of a major overhaul and renewal, it is this Canadian House of Commons. The parliamentary system in Canada, I argue, suffers from institutional retardation. Our evolution lags well behind that of Westminster and behind the parliamentary system which has evolved in the federal state of Australia.
A reformed Senate, elected, equally representing the regions, and a reinvigorated and renewed House of Commons, I believe, would give Canadians a better kind of representation, and I think they deserve much better than what our institutions allow at the present time.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I commence this debate, I would certainly like to pay tribute to
the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). Although he may be a senior citizen, I do not know of anyone who is a harder working individual. His energy, integrity and dedication are certainly an inspiration to all of us.
The Hon. Member's motion for an elected, equal and effective Senate has certainly captured the imagination of not only western Canada but of all Canada. As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup (Mr. Plourde), mentioned earlier in debate, the Meech Lake Accord is a major step toward that evolution, a Triple-E Senate.
I would like to speak about how we got to the Senate. I would like to refer to a paper prepared by Sean Graham from Calgary. He stated that the Constitution Act of 1867 stated two objectives of the Senate. The first was to bestow power to the less populous provinces so as to protect them from the heavy populated provinces and the second was to act as a chamber of second thought. Obviously, we will have to investigate whether or not the wishes of the founding fathers were fulfilled. I think it is obvious that they were not.
The British North American Act of 1867 dealt with the composition, powers and responsibilities of the Senate. Section 22 states that Canada was to consist of three divisions: Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Each division was to have 24 members. Sections 26 and 27 state that any additional members added to the Senate were to be added equally to each division, thereby maintaining equilibrium between the divisions. Section 147 states that in the case of the admission of Newfoundland or Prince Edward Island, each would receive four members in the Senate. In the event that Prince Edward Island entered Confederation, she would be considered part of the maritime region. The BN A Act of 1915 recognized the west as an independent division and granted it 24 Senators.
I would now like to quote Canada's first Prime Minister, John A. Macdonald, who said the following during the Confederation debate:
There would be no use of an Upper House if it did not exercise, when it thought proper, the right of opposing or amending or postponing the legislation of the Lower House. It would be of no value whatever were it a mere chamber for registering the decrees of the Lower House. It must be an independent House, having a free will of its own, for it is only valuable as being a regulating body, calmly considering the legislation initiated by the popular branch, and preventing any hasty or ill-considered legislation which may come from that body.
He added further:
No Ministry can in the future do what they have done in Canada before-they cannot with the view of carrying any measure, or of strengthening the party, attempt to overrule the independent opinion of the Upper House by filling it with a number of its partisans and political supporters. .. The fact of the government being prevented from exceeding a limited number will preserve the independence of the Upper House, and make it, in reality, a separate and distinct chamber, having a legitimate and controlling influence in the legislation of the country.
May 5, 1987

Let us look at what has happened since those debates in the intervening 120-odd years. I would now like to quote the words of James K. Gray who addressed the Calgary Chamber of Commerce on February 17. He stated:
In World War I the price of wheat began to mount and the government of day froze the price; cut the top off the boom and extracted from the farmers of Western Canada a disproportionate contribution to the war effort.
He stated further:
In World War II it happened again! All prices were frozen, but at the time the freeze was introduced farm prices were still at the late-depression levels and the booming world prices, which could have provided an opportunity for our farm operators to clear debt and consolidate their operations, were withheld.
It happened again in peacetime between 1972 and 1985 when the central Government cut the top off the oil and gas boom. National policies on oil and gas reduced the revenues that would have flowed to the producing provinces by $56 billion. That $56 billion would have gone to the producing provinces and the producing companies. Instead, these revenues were passed on to the consumers of Canada and to the federal Treasury. That is what has happened. That is why the people of western Canada are demanding a stronger say in the system.
A number of people have looked at reform of the Senate. I would like to list some of the groups of people who have spoken out in this respect in the last eight years. The Canada West Foundation put out a report entitled Alternatives in 1978. The B.C. Government put out a constitutional report in 1978. There was an Ontario Government advisory committee in 1978 which dealt with the subject, as well as a federal government amendment Bill of 1978. There were the Conservative policy proposals in 1978, as well as an article by the Canadian Bar Association in 1979. The Pepin-Robarts task force called for reform of the Senate. The Canada West Foundation put out a regional representations paper in 1980 on this topic. The Joint Committee of the House of Commons and Senate on Senate Reform published its report in 1984. The Alberta Legislative Committee on Senate Reform issued its report in 1985, and the Macdonald Royal Commission published its report in 1986. There is no doubt that through this debate more and more people are looking at it and saying: "We have a problem. We have had this problem for 120 years. It is time that we addressed it".
What is happening in other parts of the world? In the House of Commons central Canada has 60 per cent of the seats. In terms of equal representation it would only have two parts out of 10. The West and the North have 28 per cent of the seats of the House of Commons, while Atlantic Canada has but 12 per cent. Essentially, then, 60 per cent of the House of Commons represents the population of central Canada in Ontario and Quebec. There are predictions that 50 per cent of Canada's population will be located in Ontario by the year 2000.
In the United States the largest state has two Senators, as does the smallest state. Switzerland has the same balance. In Australia the largest state and the smallest state each has 10
The Senate
representatives. In Germany the largest state has five Senators while the smallest has three. In Canada the largest has 24 while the smallest has four. We have a built-in imbalance in our system. This leads to alienation. To address this alienation we have to address reform of the Senate. We must move to a Triple E Senate.
I will finish my remarks as I commenced them by congratulating my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River, for bringing forward an excellent and worth-while motion.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too wish to join in the debate on the motion presented to the House by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). The Hon. Member is one with whom I at times violently agree and with whom I at times violently disagree. There is no doubt that the Hon. Member is indeed an experienced parliamentarian and that I have no trouble at all with many of his ideas. I enjoy listening to the Hon. Member when he takes a few strips off the CPR and the central banks. I sit and applaud him because I think that many of his arguments and reasons are sound. Indeed, he very often represents the sense of western Canadians. As such, I appreciate the remarks and the comments that he often makes. On this occasion I have very little difficulty in supporting the Hon. Member. The proposal for a Triple-E Senate has a lot going for it.
First we have the notion of an elected Senate. We in the NDP have always considered the appointed Senate to be an obsolete body. Imagine these people, most often appointed for purely political patronage reasons, having a say in the legislative process. That is surely a throwback to medieval times. It has no place in a modern democratic society. It is amazing that we have kept this appointed Senate for as long as we have. However, it has been, I suppose, to the advantage of the various Governments to maintain the status quo.
If we are going to have a second body, it of course should be elected. There should be no question about that. As to an equal Senate, if we are going to have a second legislative body like a Senate, then there is something to be said for it being equal. It should represent the regions of this country. The House of Commons is elected on a proportional basis, and we could have the Senate as a second body of review representing the regional interests.
In a unitary state you can make an argument that such a body is not necessary. In a federal state, however, one with continuous tensions between different regions, cultures, and, very often, points of view, to have an equal Senate allows the legislative process to take into account regional differences. I suggest that an equal Senate would facilitate a smoother functioning of Government in this federal state. I suggest that with an equal Senate it is possible that we will have less regional alienation than now exists.

May 5, 1987
The Senate
There is no question that today there is a tremendous amount of alienation in western Canada. I am sure you have heard on many occasions that our fellow Canadians out West do not feel they are really full partners in Confederation. They are and have been treated historically as second cousins. When times are good in the West, our wealth has been taken from us. There was the NEP. The previous speaker mentioned other historic cases such as during wartime where the prices of wheat and other grains were frozen, all to the betterment and advantage of the bulk of our population in central Canada. Having an equal Senate would ensure that those resource grabs will no longer occur. Western Canadians need that reassurance. It is one thing to have resources taken from you in the boom times, but in the down times we have a dickens of a job trying to get some assistance in the West.
The debate last week on the farm crisis is an illustration of the type of battle which has to occur in order to get back some of the wealth we lost in the boom times. When you survey the editorials of the eastern newspapers you find that they go on and on about how it is time that the farmers bit the bullet. They have to accept that we should have fewer farmers. These, Mr. Speaker, are fair weather friends. There are some people in central Canada who are quite willing to see great hunks of our farm population going under in these bad economic times. They are not willing to offer assistance to ensure that those farms remain viable so that when the price of wheat gets back up we will be functioning farm units.
Coming back to the question in front of us, I think an equal Senate would help in that regard. It is not a guarantee, but it is at least a step in the right direction so that all regions in this country are treated on an equal basis.
We then come to the third E, and that is effective. Again 1 have no problem with an effective Senate. There is work to be done by a second House. There is work to be done which will help contribute to wise legislation and wise governing of the country.
I am not certain about the final outcome of the conference at Meech Lake with respect to Senate reform. My initial reaction is that Senate reform will be frozen. In essence the patronage opportunity which used to belong to the governing Party on the federal level has now been transferred to the governing Parties in the provinces. Really we have replaced federal patronage with provincial patronage. As well, every province will now have a veto on Senate reform. That, I think, will make it extremely difficult to achieve Senate reform in the future. The First Ministers will be discussing Senate reform in the conferences ahead so we will know more about their attitude.
Whether the various provinces will be honest and prepared to see an effective and equal elected Senate remains to be seen. However, at this stage I feel somewhat pessimistic. I am not convinced that all the provinces will agree to Senate reform or forgo their new-found patronage opportunities and instead depend upon an elected Senate. That is why 1 was particularly surprised that the Premier of Alberta was not more forceful in trying to obtain a new agenda for Senate reform.
I accept and understand that the conference dealt primarily with obtaining some agreement to allow Quebec into the Constitution. I laud both the Government and the Premiers for their efforts and their accomplishments. However, I really had some fear that when it comes to Senate reform the agreement as it now stands will really not allow for genuine Senate reform. Certainly we do not have an elected Senate now. It will now be appointed by the provinces. We do not have an equal Senate because the distribution of Senate appointments remains as skewed as it was before, with central Canada appointing most of the Senators. We certainly do not have an agenda to allow for an effective Senate.
Again I am somewhat fearful that the way things are now we will not see genuine Senate reform in the very near future. Yet, as to the resolution in front of us, I am quite prepared to endorse it and support it and I congratulate the Hon. Member for Bow River for an excellent motion.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the opportunity to take part in this debate this afternoon on the motion put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). Like my colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary North (Mr. Gagnon), 1 have had the opportunity of working with the Hon. Member for Bow River since 1982. I certainly admire his dedication to the House and to his riding, and I appreciate the opportunity to be able to sit with him.
The motion calls for the abolition of the present Senate and its replacement by an elected Senate with equal representation for each province and territory. It also asks that intergovernmental consultations to this end commence at the earliest opportunity. The motion is certainly timely in light of the recent historic agreement reached by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Premiers at Meech Lake, Quebec, on April 30.
Calls for a directly elected Senate of some kind have grown significantly in recent years. In January, 1984, for example, a special joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate recommended a system of direct election which would give smaller provinces proportionately more Senators than populous provinces.
The joint committee also recommended that the Senate consist of 144 Members, with 24 Members each from Ontario and Quebec, 42 from the combined Atlantic provinces, 48 from the West, 4 from the Northwest Territories, and 2 from Yukon.
In March 1985, a Select Special Committee of the Alberta Legislative Assembly endorsed what has popularly become known as a Triple-E Senate, meaning direct election, equal representation by province, and effective powers. As the Alberta special committee argued, Canada needs an effective Upper House in order to protect the diverse interests of Canadians. The recommendations in that report were unanimously endorsed by the Alberta Legislature in May, 1985.
May 5, 1987

On March 10 of this year, the Alberta Legislature unanimously confirmed its support for the special committee's report.
Others have suggested looking at the Australian Senate as a means of grafting the federal principle on to a parliamentary system of government. Like the Canadian Senate, the Australian Second Chamber was intended to ensure that state interests would be taken into account with the national Government.
Senate reform and a directly elected Senate, in particular, are issues which have acquired considerable public appeal and hold great attraction to a number of political leaders in the west. There is little doubt that direct election represents, in part, a desire for a stronger voice in federal institutions. Similarly, there is some sympathy for the Triple-E proposal, though difficult questions remain about the powers of such a Senate, its relationship to the House of Commons, and its effect on the powers of provincial Governments. As noted by Professors Peter McCormick and David Elton in their March 1987 article for the Canada West Foundation entitled The Western Economy and Canadian Unity, the replacement of an existing Senate with a new elected Senate will raise a wide range of questions of detail which will have to be worked out. Nevertheless, they added:
If Canada is to maintain and enhance the opportunities for its citizens in an increasingly competitive world, it must create national institutions which are capable of acting in the interests of all Canadians.
Finally, Professors McCormick and Elton impressed upon the First Ministers the need for attention to Senate reform. They said:
We have only begun the process of the renewal of the Canadian federation, and if the impetus is lost now we may not have the luxury of waiting another century before the problems arise again.
Prior to the First Ministers' meeting at Meech Lake, Premier Getty endorsed the Triple E proposal. In his April 5 speech to the Alberta Progressive Conservative Party Convention, he declared that Canada "can only grow in a healthy way if our regional representation is fair and balanced''.
While not in any way downplaying the importance of Senate reform, on April 9 in the House the Prime Minister reminded all First Ministers of their commitment under the August 1986 Edmonton Declaration that the top constitutional priority was the following one:
-to bring about Quebec's full and active participation in the Canadian federation. There was a consensus among the Premiers that then they will pursue further constitutional discussions on matters raised, which will include, amongst other items, Senate reform, fisheries, property rights, etc.
The Prime Minister went on to say:
If the matter of Senate reform is reached pursuant to this formula enunciated by the Premiers, the Government of Canada will have a proposal to put forward in regard to Senate reform.
In this same spirit the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) injected an element of caution as we enter the second round of constitutional discussions. Speaking in Camrose, Alberta on April 25, he pointed out that many questions "have to be considered very carefully as we proceed with Senate reform because you cannot change one institution in isolation from the rest". The Minister also affirmed that "we want changes that make Canada work better, that require
The Senate
both commitment and care". He added that this was the approach in which the Government would address the undeniable need for Senate reform.
The Prime Minister and the 10 Premiers took a crucial step in strengthening the federation by reaching an agreement on the top constitutional priority-bringing Quebec into the Constitution. However, the process does not end there. The communique issued at Meech Lake on April 30 required the following:
A First Ministers' Conference on the Constitution be held not less than once per year and that the first be held within 12 months of proclamation of this amendment but not later than the end of 1988.
Among the items on the agenda to be entrenched in the Constitution will be Senate reform, including the functions and role of the Senate, the powers of the Senate, the method of selection of Senators, and the distribution of Senate seats.
Finally, as a demonstration of good faith on the part of the Prime Minister, the communique provided:
-until constitutional amendments regarding the Senate are accomplished the federal Government shall appoint persons from lists of candidates provided by provinces where vacancies occur and who are acceptable to the federal Government.
I remind Hon. Members that this change to the method of Senate appointments is a variation of numerous proposals in the past aimed at providing a role for the provinces in the selection of Senators. Among these was one put forward by the federal Government in the 1969 discussion paper entitled The Constitution and the People of Canada. The paper suggested:
The Senate could be partly selected by the federal Government and partly selected by provincial Governments. The method of selection of Senators by the provinces could be by nomination of the provincial Governments.
The Prime Minister announced the following in the House on May 1:
The Meech Lake Agreement is good for Canada and good for Canadians. It will unblock the constitutional reform process and enable Canadians to turn their attention to other issues such as Senate reform and fisheries.
The tabling and proclamation of the Meech Lake Agreement will conclude the first round of constitutional renewal. Senate reform is very much a part and indeed is at the top of the agenda of the second round.
Though much remains to be done, let us not forget that much has been accomplished. I believe, as the Prime Minister declared in his address at Sept lies, Quebec on August 6, 1984, that we are on the threshold of a true national renewal.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to debate the motion sponsored by our colleague from Bow River (Mr. Taylor) concerning the reorganization of the Senate. Perhaps it might be useful if I were to put this question in a certain historical context to make it easier to understand. First I would refer to the Charlottetown meeting of the Fathers of Confederation when these outstanding Canadians set up a parliamentary system designed to protect the interests of every region of Canada, and this was the advent of the House of Commons. They also established a Senate, and one of its objectives was to protect the interests of the various components of Canada, especially its minorities.

May 5, 1987
The Senate
Over the years Members of the House have heard a number of representations aimed at revamping and modernizing the Senate. So our Government too decided to change and modernize to take the present context into account, and particularly to correct the indecency of the previous Liberal administration which, in 1982, chose to ignore 27 per cent of the population of Canada-in other words, when the 74 Quebec Liberal Members forgot to include their province in the new constitutional agreement. Indeed it is easy to understand why they should display so little interest in anything constitutional: As I look around today I cannot see a single Member of that Party listening to what is being said in the House, proof positive that they could hardly care less about the very essence of Canada.
Our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and our Government had promised to integrate Quebec in the Canadian Confederation. A few years had elapsed since we took that stand and, recently, thanks to the cooperation of all the provincial premiers, especially Mr. Bourassa from Quebec, our Government has been able to offer Quebec full participation in the Canadian Constitution. All Quebecers are delighted with this historic meeting of April 30, 1987, which will remain for us Quebecers and I am sure for a great many other Canadians as significant a landmark as our Fathers of Confederation's meeting in Charlottetown.
The meeting was a success, Mr. Speaker, thanks to our Prime Minister, who managed to obtain a consensus from ten premiers of 10 Canadian provinces on bringing Quebec back into the constitutional fabric. Today, this country is complete, from coast to coast.
Today, I am more of a Canadian because 1 feel Canadian through and through as a result of what was achieved by my Prime Minister on April 30, 1987. We corrected the mistake and the omission the Liberals made in 1982. Furthermore, our provincial premiers and the Prime Minister of Canada decided to provide new possibilities for the provinces including a reevaluation and redefinition of the role of the Senate, and they included in the new Constitution a requirement to consider Senate reform.
They even decided, and this is to take place in 1988, to have a meeting of the 10 premiers and the Prime Minister of Canada on the subject of the functions and role of the Senate, the powers of the Senate, the method of selection of Senators and the distribution of Senate seats. Meanwhile, Mr. Speaker, to show our goodwill and receptivity to all suggestions by the various provinces that were involved in the Accord reached on
April 30, 1987, our Prime Minister has decided that he will not proceed with further appointments to the Senate before receiving a list of candidates provided by provinces where vacancies occur. We have wiped out the constitutional affront of 1982. We have wiped out Liberal arrogance. We are now Quebecers and Canadians who are proud to be part of Canada. We feel welcome.
Our Prime Minister was the first Prime Minister to formally accept provincial proposals concerning Senate appointments and to take them into account in appointing senators. What a difference with the previous liberal administration!
Think of such a move by Rene Levesque to have someone appointed at the time, and imagine the kind of cooperation that would have existed between himself and the former Prime Minister of Canada.
However, Quebecers and Canadians know there are always improvements to be made. They are needed. This is why my position is to respect a decision made by the 10 Premiers and the Prime Minister on April 30, 1987, until the next negotiation meeting on the Senate that will be held before the end of 1988.
I feel certain, Mr. Speaker, that all the First Ministers will be able at that time to reach a consensus leading to a Senate amendment that will be supported by all.
