speechtext:
The hour provided for the consideration of Private Members' Business has now expired. Pursuant to Standing Order 36(2), the order is dropped to the bottom of the order of precedence on the Order Paper.
May 5, 1987
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 66 deemed to have been moved.

I rise now to address a question that I have raised in Question Period with the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) regarding the Government's policy on film distribution. The facts are very well known to us. They are pointed out, I am afraid, in very sad detail in the report of the film industry task force which was published in November, 1985. The Government has had well over a year to consider its response. Its response has been very weak, especially considering the very serious situation that when Canadians go to see films at the cinema and pay their money, the money does not gets plowed back into Canadian film production. Because distribution outlets are overwhelmingly American-owned and because of the vertical integration within the system, the money goes mainly into American production. Only 3 per cent of the films actually seen on the screen are Canadian.
This task force came up with some very strong recommendations for reform. First, that the distribution of films and videos in all media in Canada be by companies owned and controlled by Canadians. Very specifically the Government was asked to make a clear policy statement that Canadian ownership and control over distribution in Canada is essential and to take the appropriate legislative and regulatory measures to ensure that this policy is carried out. Has the Government done it, Mr. Speaker? No, I am afraid not. It would appear from remarks made by the Minister that there is no intention to carry out this recommendation of the task force.
There are two more recommendations for specific action. One is regarding tax incentives and the third is the creation of a Canadian film fund with an annual budget of $60 million. Work on this third recommendation has been undertaken, but the fourth recommendation has also been ignored.
The fourth recommendation is to enact measures which will prevent all vertical integration, distribution and exhibition to the extent such integration limits competition and freedom of trade in Canada. The Government has taken only a very modest step in the direction of fulfilling Recommendation No. 4.
The task force composed of experts in the field concluded that its principal recommendations are relatively few. They form a whole and cannot be separated without threatening to upset the balance of the entire structure and should be applied concurrently. The task force is looking for a comprehensive response on the part of the Government and the Government has not made that comprehensive response.
Adjournment Debate
It has been estimated that the film import licensing proposal of the Minister will reduce American control by only 15 per cent or less. Instead of 97 per cent of the profits going out of the country, roughly 80 per cent of the profits would go out of the country. That is not a very significant change.
I would like to compliment the Minister for taking a step in the right direction and to point out the cowardice of the previous Liberal Government which had these facts available to it over the years. The previous Minister, Francis Fox, certainly had access to that information. Yet he turned tail and did not have the courage to stand up to the American majors who are milking money out of Canada, plowing that money back into American productions and leaving Canadians with little opportunity to see the excellent films that do get produced in Canada and a very small fund of money from which to produce more.
I note that the Minister's paper on cultural industries cites European examples of much more vigorous methods of dealing with film production and distribution. Other countries that do more include Austria, West Germany, France, Italy, The Netherlands, Australia and New Zealand, indeed all the EEC countries. Since the 1920s, these countries have protected the production and distribution of films to ensure that they have viable film industries, something which we do not have here.
Canada is treated as a colony of the United States for purposes of film distribution. It is shameful for Canadians to have to be treated within their own country as an appendage of the United States. Of course, we do not have the funds to develop our own industry.
I am afraid that the Minister's response so far has been the desire to be congratulated on the very modest step she has taken, not to look seriously at all four recommendations made by the task force. She seems to consider her step adequate. In effect, she has even repudiated the first recommendation for a Canadian-ownership and distribution policy, a policy countries larger than ours that need this protection even less have instituted.
Our Minister is not standing up to the American distribution companies and is not putting Canadian policy first. I would call on the House to ask the Minister to put Canadian distribution first so that excellent Canadian programs will be distributed and Canadians will have a chance to see them.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the Hon. Member's concerns about the distribution of films in the Canadian film industry. The Government has taken decisive action to foster the development of a healthy Canadian film industry, building on the recommendations of the film industry task force chaired by Steven Roth and Marie Josee Raymond. This means addressing all phases of the industry: production, distribution and exhibition. Our goal is to have a viable film industry so that Canadians can have access to films by Canadians about Canadians.

May 5, 1987
Adjournment Debate
In a pattern that has hardly changed in the past decade, only about 3 per cent of screen time in Canadian theatres has been devoted to Canadian films. To remedy this abnormal situation, the Government has acted on two complementary fronts. It established a new $30 million feature film fund administered by Telefilm to provide direct financial support of the production and distribution of Canadian feature films.
A stronger distribution sector is needed for two reasons; first, to bring Canadian films to Canadian screens and, second, to participate in financing the production of those films. To be strong, Canadian distribution companies have to be able to do more than distribute Canadian films. They have to be able to distribute more of the films imported into Canada.
To give Canadian distributors an equitable opportunity to distribute imported films, the Government is developing legislation to license the importation of films meant for commercial distribution in Canada. Such legislation will contribute to the establishment of Canada as a distinct market for film distribution. It will further the creation of a healthy production, distribution, exhibition cycle for Canadians and Canadian film and video productions. At present we are consulting with the Canadian film industry, the provinces and, indeed, the American film industry, the distributors of which operate in Canada on this pending legislation.
The American film industry is responsible for bringing more than $200 million in production activity into this country annually, which employs hundreds of Canadians in creative and technical positions.
Our consultations with the American film industry have drawn sympathetic support to the principles and objectives of the proposed legislation. However, we must address their existing presence in Canada with a degree of fairness while allowing Canadians the freedom of choice to see whatever movies they wish to, be they foreign or Canadian. The point of the legislation is to ensure that a significant choice is available in the market of high quality, well-promoted Canadian films to compete with foreign films. I must state that the Canadian film community is very supportive of this move by the Government of Canada.
With this legislation Canada will be treated as a separate country for purposes of the importation and distribution of films. The establishment of Canada as a separate market in North America clearly asserts our foreign identity. The Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) has announced her intention to introduce this legislation and the Government is committed to the continuing development of the indigenous Canadian cultural industries in Canada.

subtopic: TRADE-CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS- PARLIAMENTARY DEBATE ON POSSIBLE TREATY
TRADE-CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS- PARLIAMENTARY DEBATE ON POSSIBLE TREATY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know when or why you became a member of the Conservative Party. I would like to have a chat with you about that one of these days. However, I became a Member during my university days. Before doing so I went to meetings of all three of our national Parties and I listened very carefully. It was after
listening to what was said at those meetings that I decided that my own views and philosophies were best reflected in the pragmatic, socially progressive and fiscally conservative approach of the Progressive Conservative Party.
One of the most appealing corner-stones of the Progressive Conservative Party, in my view, was its Canadian nationalism. It was the Party, as you know, which created Confederation and Canada. It was the Party which established something called national policy, a tariff barrier which stretched from sea to sea and created a Canadian industrial economy.
That, in my mind, was one of the things which clearly distinguished the Progressive Conservative Party from the Liberal Party, as evidenced by the great reciprocity debate of 1911. That tariff barrier policy was established by Sir John A. Macdonald and supported and defended by Prime Ministers Robert Borden, Arthur Meighen and R. B. Bennett. It has been and is, therefore, a corner-stone of Progressive Conservative policy.
I am sure that you, Mr. Speaker, can imagine my feelings and the feelings of many other supporters of the Progressive Conservative Party when, in the summer of 1985, the Government decided to embark upon a course of trade negotiations with the United States. I know that your fears, Mr. Speaker, my fears, and those of many other members of our Party were allayed when we realized what was facing us. We realized, first, the importance of trade to Canada. Twenty-seven per cent of our Gross National Product is derived from trade. One job of every three in this country comes from trade. In fact, two jobs of every five in my native Province of Ontario come from trade.
I came to realize the wealth which trade generated and that it helped to create and maintain our social services and cultural institutions. I realized that tariffs, which had been at 30 per cent 40 years ago, had dropped to approximately 9 per cent and even 5 per cent in the case of the United States. In all that time our national wealth had increased some three times and the number of jobs in this country had doubled. At that same time, there were some 300 separate Bills before the United States Congress that are now consolidated into an omnibus trade Bill which, if passed, would seriously affect and damage Canadian trade with the United States and cause jobs to be lost in this country.
The effect of the countervail tariffs of the United States on our softwood lumber products and the effects of the antidumping actions of the United States and the escape clause actions under the GATT escape clause provisions on our shakes and shingles all made me realize that we needed some sort of protective mechanism to protect our jobs in this country. The only way we could do it would be to sit down and negotiate with the United States. To do otherwise would be to invite disaster. Canadians would never forgive us if we allowed that to happen.
May 5, 1987

At the same time, I realize that four times in the past we have successfully negotiated trade agreements with the United States: One in 1935, one in 1938, the Auto Pact and the Defence Production Sharing Agreement.
While my fears, and I know yours, have been allayed, there are other members of our Party and other people in the country who still have great concerns and fears, which I can certainly understand. One of those people is one of my constituents. She is Mrs. Mary MacMillan, who lives on Barbara Crescent. A few weeks ago she visited me to express her concerns about these trade negotiations with the United States. She expressed her fears, and the fears of many others, about the possibility of U.S. domination, a weakening of our economic and cultural sovereignty, and the possibility that these negotiations were irreversible and her inability to take this on trust and faith. She expressed her feeling that we were negotiating our future and our ability to make our own decisions as a country. Of course, she expressed her strong and deep feelings for this country which I know you and I share, Mr. Speaker.
Those feelings largely stem from the fact that we do not know much about the negotiations that are taking place. There is a lot of secrecy in those negotiations, which is understandable, because there must be secrecy in negotiations of this sort. One cannot lay one's cards on the table in a poker game, and we cannot lay them on the table perhaps the way Canadians would prefer so they would know what is going on in negotiations like this.
At the same time, that is why I believe it is very important that all of the facts and all of the terms be made public and put before Parliament, and that there be an opportunity for Parliament to approve it before that agreement is signed. I am not sure that that will allay the concerns of my constituent, Mrs. Mary MacMillan, but it will allay the concerns of many people.
That is why on September 30, 1985, I directed a question to the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and asked him if there would be that opportunity to have that information and have Parliament approve the agreement. That is why I repeated, on March 16, 1987, the same question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
The Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs made it quite clear that we would get that information, that it would be placed before Parliament and there would be an opportunity to approve it. In his remarks, the Prime Minister seemed to modify that somewhat when he said:
There shall be no treaty signed until such time as Members of the House of
Commons have been apprised of it and have been given an opportunity to
speak to it.
Tonight I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will clarify that once and for all, and advise us and all Canadians that before an agreement is signed with the United States we will know all the terms, all of the letters of understanding, and all of the side
Adjournment Debate
agreements if there are any, and that the House will have an opportunity to approve it before that agreement is signed.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: TRADE-CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS- PARLIAMENTARY DEBATE ON POSSIBLE TREATY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree you are a very understanding and sharing Speaker as remarked upon by my friend, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway). 1 must say that this was one of the better speeches I have heard on the trade negotiations and I want to congratulate the Hon. Member.
I understand the concern of the Canadian people in these trade negotiations. It is new territory. It is a large comprehensive trade agreement which is very important to the future of Canada. I might point out that although we are in many ways examining new areas, we are doing what I think is some very imaginative work. I go back to the opposition Parties which keep opposing what we are doing but do not come up with any alternative to the status quo, which we feel is just not right.
The question of provincial involvement, I believe, is one which has to be addressed in the approval system. We are bringing the provinces right along on these trade negotiations. The First Ministers meet regularly. They met recently in March and two meetings are scheduled for June and September. We must realize that the federal Government has jurisdiction over international treaties but there may be within the agreement some necessity for provinces to agree in areas of jurisdiction which will affect them directly.
The provinces have agreed with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to work right along with the federal Government in deciding on a ratification process a little later on.

As to whether Parliament can scrutinize and approve any trade agreement reached with the United States, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) already stated in this House that no agreement will be signed until Hon. Members have been informed of its contents and had an opportunity to comment.

1 can assure the Hon. Member as well that with an agreement will come legislation, obviously, which will have to be brought to the House of Commons. At that time approval will have to be given by this House of Commons.

subtopic: HARBOUR FRONT-MORATORIUM ON CONSTRUCTION PROJECTS AT TORONTO WATERFRONT. (B) TYPES OF PROJECTS INVOLVED
HARBOUR FRONT-MORATORIUM ON CONSTRUCTION PROJECTS AT TORONTO WATERFRONT. (B) TYPES OF PROJECTS INVOLVED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 13, I asked a question about the Government's announcement of a moratorium on property development on the Harbourfront site in Toronto. Since the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) was not in the House that day, his colleague, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mrs. Vezina) took notice of my question. I am raising it again today because I think the issue is an important one.

May 5, 1987
Adjournment Debate
Hon. Members will recall that both the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) and the Minister of Public Works had announced that certain development projects at Elarbourfront would be halted pending a review of its development policy. The Secretary of State announced there would be a total freeze on projects without City of Toronto building permits. However, the Minister of Public Works announced that some projects would be permitted to go ahead.
These two statements were made on a Friday. One of the Ministers left that day on business outside the country and the other Minister was absent from the House when I asked my question the following Monday. On April 15, two days later, the Minister of Public Works issued a press release which did not resolve the confusion created by the two statements.
There are a number of projects on the Harbourfront property in various stages of development. Whether or not they are going ahead depended on which statement was the real indication of the Government's intent. Some of the projects are commercial developments, including a proposal for a 40-storey office tower. Some are high-rise residential developments and condominiums.
As well, there is a co-operative housing project and two condominium projects on the Bathurst Quay which are meant for seniors and low-income families. Affordable rent and accommodation is badly needed in downtown Toronto. However, from the two statements issued by the Government it was not possible to tell whether these projects would be going ahead or not. It was not possible to tell which of the other projects would be affected by the moratorium.
I also asked for the Government's reasons in calling a moratorium. There was considerable media speculation. It would have been useful to have had a clear statement from the Minister in the House at the time.
Questions have been raised and concerns expressed about how Harbourfront, which is a Crown corporation, is interpreting its development policy. I realize that as a Crown corporation it is expected to act autonomously, but the situation appears to have developed to the point where Harbourfront was going its own way and everyone else was in the dark-the Government of Canada which owns the site and the City of Toronto which, through its official plan, zoning and building by-laws, is supposed to control its building permits, building height, density and so on.
Public concern grew with the construction of a couple of high-rise condominium towers on a relatively small parcel of Harbourfront land, and as the pace of development in general accelerated.
I assume these are some of the reasons why the Government has undertaken a review at this time. It seems that the
Government rushed to get the review under way and to announce it to the media. However, no information was given about the terms of the review or the expected date of completion. It seems that the situation had got so far out of hand that the Government was forced to impose a moratorium to get some control over it.
I assume that the review is proceeding. I am sure that the Government will make some sort of announcement in due course by press release, but Torontonians are vitally interested in knowing when the review is to be completed. I trust that the Parliamentary Secretary this evening will inform the House of the actions that the Government proposes to take.
Harbourfront was intended to be a balanced mix of development, open space and cultural activities for Toronto residents and visitors. It is clear that the desired balance is not there. I trust that the Parliamentary Secretary will take this opportunity to give some information about the action the Government has taken to date, as well as its intentions for the future with regard to Harbourfront.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: HARBOUR FRONT-MORATORIUM ON CONSTRUCTION PROJECTS AT TORONTO WATERFRONT. (B) TYPES OF PROJECTS INVOLVED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I trust the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) as a Torontonian will allow a Bramptonian, a neighbour who uses the facilities of Harbourfront quite often, to reply on behalf of the Minister. I might say, first, that I have a special interest in the Toronto waterfront, having been a former employee of Ontario Place Corporation. 1 have watched with interest, sometimes with pleasure and sometimes with displeasure, the development of the water-front. It is fair to say that the questions raised by the Hon. Member are those that concern the Government. Thus, a policy review and a suspension of new developments at Harbourfront was announced by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) on April 15.
The purpose of the halt is to respect the review of Harbourfront program, which is currently being carried out by the city, as well as to support the federal policy review. In making the announcement, the Minister stated that clarification of the application of the suspension would be issued within 30 days. The clarification is as follows.
First, all projects which have received building permits and are now under construction may proceed. There are no projects currently under construction which have not received their building permits. Second, Harbourfront Corporation will obtain the advice and comments of the City of Toronto on all projects which have yet to receive the requisite Government of Canada approvals.
Third, for those projects which may still require City of Toronto approvals, further Harbourfront and Government of
May 5, 1987

Canada consideration will also await receipt of the city's advice and comments.
In its review of the Harbourfront program, the City of Toronto established the Harbourfront Review Committee as a mechanism for obtaining input from interested groups and individuals. Advice and comments passed to the Government of Canada by the city will be based in part on this input. In addition, Harbourfront Corporation itself is planning to hold a series of public forums to debate issues surrounding its role and mandate. These public forums will begin in the first week of June at Harbourfront.
1 guess it is a matter of opinion as to whether there is a good balance of the various areas which make up our waterfront in Toronto. There are some very exciting cultural activities that go on down there. Within the last few weeks there was a major
Adjournment Debate
debate on capital punishment held down there. It is being used by the public. I share the concerns of the Hon. Member, as I think the Government does. We want to ensure that the development that does take place down there is proper, that we have a good mix, and that the public can still go down and participate in the myriad of attractions which take place at Harbourfront.
